title: Find Missing Constants in Equivalent Expressions with Regression
description: Use Desmos regression with a list of allowed input values to find missing constants in expressions that are equivalent for every permitted value of the variable.
authoring_notes: Reverse-drift export 2026-08-26: reconstructed from the production lesson 4c22e546-2a07-4ffc-8f99-a2f3e3b21f59 (md5-verified block dump) so the repo is the source of truth again. Block ids without semantic names were authored in-app; generated ids follow block_type_N.

blocks.html:
What did Desmos discover?

The two expressions in the calculator are equivalent for every value of \(x\). In the first line, the input variable has been written as \(x_1\), and the equals sign has been replaced by the regression symbol ~.

Look below the regression. Find the values Desmos assigns to \(a\) and \(b\).

Notice: The second line gives \(x_1\) three different values at once.

content.hint: Read the assignments shown directly below the regression line.
content.prompt: Which values does Desmos assign to the missing constants in \(ax^2+bx+6\)?
content.explanation: Right. Desmos finds \(a=3\) and \(b=9\). Those values make \(ax^2+bx+6\) equivalent to \(3(x+1)(x+2)\).

blocks.html:
Recognize this question type

The move: Define the input as a list of allowed values, then regress.

Why it pays: "Equivalent for every value of \(x\)" questions become a fit instead of an expansion, so there are no sign slips left to make.

One caution: If the regression panel starts assigning a value to your input variable, you forgot to define it as a list. That's the tell.

Look for two expressions in one variable. One expression contains missing constants such as \(a\) and \(b\); the other has no missing constants but is written in a different form.

The question may say the expressions are equivalent, one can be rewritten as the other, or an equation is true for all values of the variable.

Instead of asking for the constants separately, the question often asks for a combination such as \(a/b\), \(ab\), or \(2a-b\).

Key idea: The two expressions must match for many input values, not just one.

content.hint: Look for missing constants inside one expression and wording that says two expressions match for every input.
content.prompt: Which problem is the best match for this regression strategy?
choices: Simplify the expression \(x^2-25\) and list every one of its factors.
The expression \(a(x+2)+b\) is equivalent to \(4x+11\) for all \(x\). Find \(a+b\).
Find the equation of the line through two given points, or any equivalent form.
Estimate the mean of a small data set of measured values.
content.explanation: Correct. The letters \(a\) and \(b\) are missing constants, and the equivalence must hold for all \(x\).

blocks.html:
Separate the input from the missing constants

In \(a(x+2)+b\), the letters have different jobs:

  • \(x\) is the input variable. The identity must work for many values of \(x\).
  • \(a\) and \(b\) are the missing constants. Desmos should find one fixed value for each.

Keep the constant names exactly as the question gives them. Because lowercase \(x\) and \(y\) are reserved for graphing in Desmos, change an input named \(x\) to \(x_1\) or an input named \(y\) to \(y_1\). Leave other input variables, such as \(t\), unchanged.

content.hint: Which letter is allowed to vary while the missing constants stay fixed?
content.prompt: In the identity \(p(t+4)+q(t-1)=5t+10\), which letter should become a list in Desmos?
choices: \(p\), because it appears first in the identity
\(q\), because it is the subtracted constant
Both \(p\) and \(q\) at the same time
\(t\), because it is the input variable
content.explanation: Exactly. The identity must work for many values of \(t\), so define \(t\) as a list. Only inputs named \(x\) or \(y\) need a subscript because those letters are reserved for graphing. Desmos will solve for the fixed constants \(p\) and \(q\).

blocks.html:
Why one input value is not enough

If you test only \(x=2\), the identity from the opening example becomes \(4a+2b+6=36\). Many pairs of \(a\) and \(b\) can satisfy that one equation.

But equivalent expressions must agree at many inputs. Giving \(x_1\) a list makes Desmos compare the two expressions at several values at the same time. That extra evidence pins down the constants.

Watch out: If the regression panel assigns a value to the input variable, you forgot to define the input as a list.

content.hint: Think about what “equivalent for all values” means.
content.prompt: Why do you enter \(x_1=[2,3,4]\) instead of letting Desmos choose one value of \(x_1\)?
choices: Equivalent expressions must match at many input values, and one value may not determine every constant.
A list changes the two equivalent expressions into one equation with a missing constant.
Regression cannot use positive input values unless they are supplied in a list.
The SAT requires the specific input values 2, 3, and 4 for this question type.
content.explanation: Right. Several input values force one set of constants to make the expressions agree repeatedly. The particular values are flexible as long as they are allowed.

blocks.html:
The setup: match, rename if needed, list

  1. Match the expressions. Put the missing-constants expression on one side and the provided expression on the other. Use ~ instead of =.
  2. Rename only x or y. Replace every input \(x\) with \(x_1\) or every input \(y\) with \(y_1\), because lowercase x and y are reserved for graphing. Leave another input, such as \(t\), unchanged.
  3. Give the input a list. On a new line, define several allowed values, such as x₁=[2,3,4] or t=[2,3,4].

Setup pattern: expression with constants ~ equivalent expression; then the input variable = a list.

The finish: read, calculate, answer

  1. Read the constants. The regression panel displays the values Desmos found.
  2. Type the requested combination. If the question asks for \(ab\), enter a*b on a new calculator line. If it asks for \(a/b\), enter a/b.
  3. Report that result. The constants remain assigned, so Desmos performs the final calculation for you.

Do not stop after reading \(a\) and \(b\). Answer exactly what the question asks.

Model the complete setup

Suppose \(ax^2+bx+6\) is equivalent to \(3(x+1)(x+2)\), and the question asks for \(a/b\).

  1. Enter ax₁²+bx₁+6~3(x₁+1)(x₁+2).
  2. Enter x₁=[2,3,4].
  3. Read \(a=3\) and \(b=9\).
  4. On a new line, enter a/b.

Desmos evaluates the requested expression as \(1/3\).

calculator.title: Type a/b on the next line

content.hint: Use ~ between the expressions and make t—not a missing constant—the list. Since t is not reserved for graphing, it does not need a subscript.
content.prompt: Which two-line setup correctly finds \(p\) and \(q\) if \(p(t+4)+q(t-1)\) is equivalent to \(5t+10\)?
content.explanation: Correct. The regression adjusts \(p\) and \(q\) while testing the identity at \(t=0,1,2\). Only x and y need to be changed to subscripted inputs.

blocks.html:
Three ways to create the input list

Any of these can give regression several inputs:

  • Choose the values: x₁=[2,3,4]. This is the most controlled method when the allowed and forbidden values are already known.
  • Generate n random values: x₁=random(5). The function produces five values between \(0\) and \(1\). Use it when a restricted value is not known yet—for example, when \(x-b\) is in a denominator and regression still needs to find \(b\). An exact collision is highly unlikely.
  • Use consecutive integers: x₁=[1...10]. This quickly creates the values 1 through 10 when that whole range is allowed.

Choose intentionally: Use an explicit list for known restrictions; use random(n) when a forbidden value depends on a missing constant.

content.hint: Choose the method whose values lie between 0 and 1 and are very unlikely to equal the still-unknown value of b.
content.prompt: A denominator contains \(x-b\), so the forbidden input depends on the missing constant \(b\). Which list method is most useful before \(b\) is known?
content.explanation: Right. \(random(5)\) creates five values between 0 and 1. When the forbidden input depends on the unknown \(b\), an exact random collision is highly unlikely.

blocks.html:
Choose only allowed inputs

Before creating the list, inspect the original expressions and the question's conditions.

  • If a denominator contains \(x-2\), do not include \(2\).
  • If the question says \(x>2\), every list value must be greater than \(2\).
  • If a square root requires a nonnegative input, stay inside its domain.

For an identity with denominator \(x-2\) and condition \(x>2\), a safe line is x₁=[3,4,5].

Watch out: A forbidden value can make the regression undefined or unreliable.

content.hint: Every value must be greater than 2, and 2 itself makes the denominator zero.
content.prompt: The expressions contain \(1/(x-2)\), and the question states \(x>2\). Which list is safest?
content.explanation: Correct. The values 3, 4, and 5 satisfy \(x>2\) and keep \(x-2\) nonzero.

blocks.html:
Model a restricted rational identity

For \(x>2\), suppose

\[\frac{ax+b}{x-2}\]

is equivalent to

\[3+\frac{5}{x-2}.\]

The setup uses safe values:

  • (ax₁+b)/(x₁-2)~3+5/(x₁-2)
  • x₁=[3,4,5]

Desmos finds \(a=3\) and \(b=-1\). If the question asks for \(a-b\), enter a-b to get \(4\).

content.hint: Type the requested expression exactly. Desmos still remembers the assigned constants.
content.prompt: The regression assigns \(a=3\) and \(b=-1\). What should you enter if the question asks for \(a-b\)?
content.explanation: Exactly. Entering \(a-b\) uses the stored values: \(3-(-1)=4\).

blocks.html:
Error: “x may not be used as a regression parameter”

This message means the ordinary graphing variable \(x\) is still in the regression.

Fix it: replace every input \(x\) in both expressions with \(x_1\). Then define \(x_1\) as a list on a separate line.

For a problem using \(y\), use \(y_1\) in both expressions and define a list for \(y_1\).

content.hint: The error names the ordinary graphing variable x.
content.prompt: Desmos says “x may not be used as a regression parameter.” What should you check first?
choices: Whether the requested final answer involves division by a constant
Whether every input x was changed to x₁ and x₁ was defined as a list
Whether the correct answer happens to be the first choice listed
Whether the missing constants were replaced by specific numbers
content.explanation: Correct. Use \(x_1\) throughout the regression, then define \(x_1\) as a list. Keep the missing constants as letters for Desmos to find.

blocks.html:
Error: the panel assigns the input variable

Suppose the panel shows values for \(a\), \(b\), and the input variable. Desmos treated the input as another unknown constant instead of testing many values.

Fix it: add a separate list definition such as x₁=[2,3,4] or t=[2,3,4]. After that, the panel should assign only the missing constants, while the input remains the list you supplied.

content.hint: The input variable should contain several values supplied by the student, not one value chosen by regression.
content.prompt: The regression panel displays \(a=2\), \(b=7\), and \(t=4.6\). What is the most likely setup mistake?
choices: The student used too many allowed values.
The student already calculated the requested expression.
The student forgot to define \(t\) as a list.
The student should replace \(a\) and \(b\) with \(x\) and \(y\).
content.explanation: Right. Add a line such as \(t=[0,1,2]\). Then regression tests several inputs while solving only for the missing constants. Since t is not reserved for graphing, no subscript is needed.

targeted_hints.message_html: You need three lines: the regression, the input list, and \(2p+q\).
Use only the regression, the input list, and \(2p+q\).
Enter all three required lines before checking your work.

feedback.retry_message_html: Use exactly three lines: the regression, \(t=[0,1,2]\), and the requested calculation \(2p+q\).
feedback.success_message_html: Good work. Desmos uses the list to find \(p=3\) and \(q=2\), then evaluates \(2p+q=8\) on the third line.

content.instructions_html:
The expression \(p(t+4)+q(t-1)\) is equivalent to \(5t+10\) for all \(t\), and the question asks for \(2p+q\).

  1. Enter the expressions with ~ between them.
  2. On a second line, enter t=[0,1,2].
  3. After regression assigns \(p\) and \(q\), enter 2p+q on a third line.

content.hint: Type \(2p+q\) using the values Desmos stored.
content.prompt: What result did Desmos display for \(2p+q\) on the third line?

content.title: Build the restricted identity

targeted_hints.message_html: You need three lines: the regression, the safe list, and \(a-b\).
Use only the regression, the safe list, and \(a-b\).

feedback.retry_message_html: Use exactly three lines: the regression with \(x_1\), the safe list \(x_1=[3,4,5]\), and the requested calculation \(a-b\).
feedback.success_message_html: Strong work. The inputs are safe, regression finds \(a=3\) and \(b=-1\), and the third line evaluates \(a-b=4\).

content.instructions_html:
For \(x>2\), \(\frac{ax+b}{x-2}\) is equivalent to \(3+\frac{5}{x-2}\). Find \(a-b\).

  1. Enter the expressions as a regression using \(x_1\).
  2. On a second line, enter the safe list x₁=[3,4,5].
  3. After regression assigns \(a\) and \(b\), enter a-b on a third line.

content.hint: Subtracting a negative adds its opposite: \(3-(-1)\).
content.prompt: What result did Desmos display for \(a-b\) on the third line?
content.explanation: Exactly. \(a-b=3-(-1)=4\). You built the regression, protected the domain, and answered the requested combination.

content.hint: Recall the five actions: regression symbol, rename x or y if needed, safe list, constant assignments, requested calculation.
content.prompt: Without looking back, which sequence correctly finds missing constants in equivalent expressions?
choices: Use =, let Desmos choose one input value on its own, and report the first constant assignment shown for the expression.
Use ~, change x or y to a subscripted input, define a list of allowed inputs, read the constant assignments, and evaluate the requested expression.
Replace each letter, constants included, with its own list, graph both sides, and read the intersection.
Use ~ with the ordinary letter x, include the forbidden input values in the list, and round the constants to integers.
content.explanation: You have it. That sequence makes the expressions match at several valid inputs and then uses the stored constants to answer exactly what the SAT asks. Inputs other than x or y keep their original names.

content.prompt: Independent practice 1 of 5: The expression \(p(t+2)+q(t-1)\) is equivalent to \(5t+7\) for all \(t\). What is \(p-q\)?
Independent practice 2 of 5: The expression \(a(y-3)+b\) is equivalent to \(4y+2\) for all \(y\). What is \(a+b\)?
Independent practice 3 of 5: An identity contains \(1/(x-b)\), where \(b\) is a missing constant, and no other restriction is given. Which definition is the best starting list while \(b\) is unknown?
Independent practice 4 of 5: An identity contains \(1/(x+4)\), and the question specifies \(x<0\). Which input list is valid?
Independent practice 5 of 5: The expression \(z^2+az+b\) is equivalent to \((z+4)(z-3)\) for all \(z\). What is \(ab\)?
The expression \(a(x-2)+b(x+1)\) is equivalent to \(5x-7\) for all values of \(x\). What is the value of \(a\)?
content.hint: Set up the regression with \(x_1\) and \(\sim\), give \(x_1\) a list of allowed values, and read the assignment for \(a\) — not \(b\).
content.explanation: Correct. Matching the identity gives \(a+b=5\) and \(-2a+b=-7\), so \(a=4\) (and \(b=1\)). In Desmos, \(a(x_1-2)+b(x_1+1)\sim5x_1-7\) with \(x_1=[1,2,3]\) assigns the same values; \(1\) is \(b\), the wrong quantity.

content.html:
You can find missing constants with regression

You can recognize an equivalent-expression identity, rename x or y when needed, create a safe input list, diagnose common Desmos errors, read the missing constants, and calculate the requested combination.
